title: The DAP decision
primary_topics: Foundational DAP decision doctrinal column July 6, 2014 -- first CJP column after Araullo v. Aquino July 1, 2014 ruling
Justice Lucas P. Bersamin identified as ponente; 'four acts and practices under DAP, NBC No. 541 and related issuances' (not DAP itself) declared unconstitutional
Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov 13, 2013) PDAF-plainly-unconstitutional contrast vs Araullo's acts-and-practices-only striking

GAA backgrounder: five revenue sources enumerated -- (1) taxes (2) capital revenues (sales of assets) (3) grants (4) extraordinary income (gov-corp dividends) (5) borrowings; current budget P2T total; SSS/GSIS dividends as unprogrammed-funds example

World Bank-cited DAP-success quote (p.36): 'continued implementation of the DAP strengthened growth by 11.8% year on year while infrastructure spending rebounded from 29% contraction to 34% growth as of September 2013'
Constitutional ban: 'No public money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law' + 'No law shall be passed authorizing the transfer of appropriations'

Power-of-augmentation as 'one limited exception' -- President + SP + Speaker + CJ + ConCom-heads 'may, by law, be authorized to augment any item in the GAA for their respective offices from savings in other items of their respective appropriations'

FOUR unconstitutional acts: (1) only 'actual savings' transferable -- three definitions: (a) PAPs completed/discontinued/abandoned (b) vacant positions + leaves-without-pay (c) lesser cost from improved-systems-and-efficiencies; transfers 'prior to the end of the fiscal year' meeting none of these are unconstitutional

(2) Same-branch-only -- cross-border transfers (executive → Congress, Comelec, COA) unconstitutional; (3) Non-GAA PAP funding unconstitutional -- augmentation only from existing-item to existing-item; (4) Unprogrammed-funds-without-national-treasurer-certification (that revenue collections exceeded total revenue targets) unconstitutional

Operative-fact doctrine p.87 application -- acts done in good faith prior to unconstitutionality declaration remain valid; bridge-construction example; 'May the President, the author of the augmentation, be impeached?' rhetorical-close-via-deferral ('impeachment is more political than legal, so I will leave it to the politicians')
sub_topics: Araullo v. Aquino (July 1, 2014, penned by Justice Lucas P. Bersamin) declared unconstitutional four 'acts and practices under the Disbursement Acceleration Program, National Budget Circular No. 541 and related issuances'
Did NOT declare DAP unconstitutional, only 'acts and practices under' it
Unlike Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov 13, 2013) which plainly declared PDAF unconstitutional
Four are worded in deep legalese and need to be explained for lay readers
Backgrounder: annually, Congress approves General Appropriations Act (GAA) or budget
Contains estimate of revenues and funding sources, usually:
(1) taxes
(2) capital revenues (proceeds from sales of assets)
(3) grants
(4) extraordinary income (dividends of government corporations)
(5) borrowings
Budget also contains itemized public expenditures allotted to three main branches and independent agencies (COA, Comelec, Ombudsman, etc)
Current budget totals about P2 trillion
Often estimated revenues are exceeded by actual receipts -- excess funds referred to as 'unprogrammed funds'
Examples: unexpected large dividends from SSS and GSIS
Often, too, estimated expenditures are not spent -- hence 'savings' occur
DAP aims to pool these unspent funds and use them to fund projects that stimulate economy
Citing World Bank, SC decision (p.36) acknowledged program's success
'continued implementation of the DAP strengthened growth by 11.8% year on year while infrastructure spending rebounded from a 29% contraction to a 34% growth as of September 2013'
Constitution states: 'No public money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law'
Also: 'No law shall be passed authorizing the transfer of appropriations'
Under these provisions, money allotted for one PAP cannot be spent for another PAP even if both are in GAA
Congress cannot even authorize 'the transfer of appropriations' from one budget item to another
However, Constitution allows one limited exception:

'President, President of Senate, Speaker of House, CJ, and heads of Constitutional Commissions may, by law, be authorized to augment any item in the GAA for their respective offices from savings in other items of their respective appropriations'
This exception called power of augmentation
Bulk of DAP funds may have been pooled in strict adherence to this exception
However, Court found four 'acts and practices' violated it:
(1) Only 'actual savings' may be transferred from one budget item to another item in GAA
Savings are 'actual' only when:
(a) PAPs (projects, activities or programs) for which appropriation had been authorized was completed, finally discontinued, or abandoned
(b) there were vacant positions and leaves of absence without pay
(c) required or planned targets, programs and services were realized at lesser cost because of implementation of measures resulting in improved systems and efficiencies (p.59)
Thus, 'act or practice' of transferring funds 'prior to the end of the fiscal year' which did not meet any of those three instances were deemed unconstitutional
(2) Augmentation can be made only for items allocated 'for their respective offices' -- within same branch or office
Thus, 'act or practice' of transferring savings from executive to Congress, or to Comelec, or to COA, being 'cross-border' transfers, were declared unconstitutional
(3) Funding of PAPs not covered by any appropriation in GAA is also unconstitutional
Augmentation can be made only from one existing item to another existing item in budget
President cannot use budgeted funds for PAPs not found in GAA
(4) Unconstitutional also is use of unprogrammed funds in absence of legally required certification by national treasurer
That revenue collections exceeded 'total of the revenue targets'
As rule, an unconstitutional 'act or practice' is void and cannot give rise to any right or obligation
However, Court held that exception to this rule, the old 'doctrine of operative fact,' should be applied 'in the implementation of the DAP' (p.87)
Under this doctrine, acts done in good faith pursuant to a law or executive act that is later declared unconstitutional would remain valid and enforceable
Also applies when nullification of such acts would result in injustice
In short, unconstitutionality has prospective effects only
Example: bridge constructed from illegally augmented funds -- government officials who supervised in good faith construction cannot be forced to reimburse government
Neither may injustice be heaped on suppliers of construction materials by refusing to pay them
May the President, the 'author' of the augmentation, be impeached?
Court did not take that up -- neither will CJP
Impeachment is more political than legal -- so CJP will leave it to politicians

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the foundational doctrinal column on the just-released DAP decision -- the first of his July-2014 trio (A407 July 6 → A405 July 20 → A404 July 27), framed as legalese-to-lay-readers explainer. Araullo v. Aquino (July 1, 2014, penned by Justice Lucas P. Bersamin) declared unconstitutional four 'acts and practices under the Disbursement Acceleration Program, National Budget Circular No. 541 and related issuances.' It did not declare the DAP unconstitutional, only the 'acts and practices under' it, unlike Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov 13, 2013) which plainly declared the PDAF unconstitutional. The four are worded in deep legalese and need to be explained for lay readers. Backgrounder: annually, Congress approves the General Appropriations Act (GAA) or budget. In general, it contains an estimate of revenues and funding sources, which are usually (1) taxes, (2) capital revenues (like proceeds from the sales of assets), (3) grants, (4) extraordinary income (like dividends of government corporations) and (5) borrowings. The budget also contains itemized public expenditures allotted to the three main branches of government (executive, legislative and judicial) and the independent agencies (COA, Comelec, Office of the Ombudsman, etc.); the current budget totals about P2 trillion. Often, estimated revenues are exceeded by actual receipts -- these excess funds are referred to as 'unprogrammed funds' (e.g., unexpected large dividends from SSS and GSIS); often too, estimated expenditures are not spent, hence 'savings' occur. The DAP aims to pool these unspent funds and use them to fund projects that stimulate the economy. Citing the World Bank, the SC decision (p.36) acknowledged the program's success, saying that 'the continued implementation of the DAP strengthened growth by 11.8% year on year while infrastructure spending rebounded from a 29% contraction to a 34% growth as of September 2013.' Unconstitutional acts: the Constitution states, 'No public money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law.' Also, 'No law shall be passed authorizing the transfer of appropriations...' Under these provisions, money allotted for one program, activity or project (PAP) cannot be spent for another PAP even if both are in the GAA; Congress cannot even authorize 'the transfer of appropriations' from one budget item to another. However, the Constitution allows one limited exception: '...The President, the President of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and the heads of the Constitutional Commissions may, by law, be authorized to augment any item in the [GAA] for their respective offices from savings in other items of their respective appropriations.' This exception is called the power of augmentation. The bulk of DAP funds may have been pooled in strict adherence to this exception. However, the Court found that these four 'acts and practices' violated it: (1) Only 'actual savings' may be transferred from one budget item to another item in the GAA; savings are 'actual' only when '(a) the PAPs for which the appropriation had been authorized was completed, finally discontinued, or abandoned; or (b) there were vacant positions and leaves of absence without pay; or (c) the required or planned targets, programs and services were realized at a lesser cost because of the implementation of measures resulting in improved systems and efficiencies' (p.59); thus, the 'act or practice' of transferring funds 'prior to the end of the fiscal year' that did not meet any of those three instances was deemed unconstitutional. (2) Augmentation can be made only for items allocated 'for their respective offices' -- within the same branch or office; thus, the 'act or practice' of transferring savings from the executive to Congress, or to Comelec, or to COA, being 'cross-border' transfers, was declared unconstitutional. (3) Funding of PAPs not covered by any appropriation in the GAA is unconstitutional because augmentation can be made only from one existing item to another existing item -- the President cannot use budgeted funds for PAPs not found in the GAA. (4) Unconstitutional also is the use of unprogrammed funds in the absence of a legally required certification by the national treasurer that the revenue collections exceeded the 'total of the revenue targets.' Accountability: as a rule, an unconstitutional 'act or practice' is void and cannot give rise to any right or obligation; however, the Court held that the exception to this rule, the old 'doctrine of operative fact,' should be applied 'in the implementation of the DAP' (p.87) -- under this doctrine, acts done in good faith pursuant to a law or executive act that is later declared unconstitutional would remain valid and enforceable; it also applies when the nullification of such acts would result in an injustice; in short, unconstitutionality has prospective effects only. Example: a bridge is constructed from illegally augmented funds -- the government officials who supervised in good faith the construction cannot be forced to reimburse the government, and neither may injustice be heaped on suppliers of construction materials by refusing to pay them. May the President, the 'author' of the augmentation, be impeached? The Court did not take that up -- neither will CJ; impeachment is more political than legal, so CJ will leave it to the politicians.
